newsitem.title: USA: Judge refuses to step down in Butler tobacco case.
newsitem.headline: Judge refuses to step down in Butler tobacco case.

text.p: The judge in a $650 million lawsuit against cigarette makers on Thursday refused a tobacco industry request that he step down from the case, which blames second-hand smoke for the death of a Mississippi barber.

In a five-page ruling, Jones County Circuit Judge Billy Joe Landrum said the tobacco industry's motion that he disqualify himself for twice meeting plaintiffs' attorneys without a full contingent of tobacco lawyers was "not well taken and should be denied."
A lawyer for the tobacco industry said cigarette makers had not yet decided whether or not to appeal the ruling.
"We are very disappointed," attorney Wayne Drinkwater said. "We think the two conferences that occurred were the kind that should not have occurred in the absence of tobacco defendants."

Landrum has presided over the case of Burl Butler since 1994, the year the barber died of cancer. Because Butler never smoked, his family blames decades of exposure to second-hand tobacco smoke for his death and says the tobacco industry is responsible.

At a hearing on Tuesday, tobacco attorneys questioned Landrum's partiality because of meetings with plaintiff attorney Cynthia Langston that involved internal documents released by cigarette maker Liggett Group, a defendant.

The documents, part of a settlement between the Brooke Group Ltd unit and 22 state attorneys general, could be crucial to the Butler case if they support claims that tobacco companies conspired to hide the dangers of smoking.
Landrum met with Langston and Liggett attorney Thomas Cook on March 20 and 24 to ensure that all the documents were in place for possible use in the Butler suit.

But attorneys for the other defendants said they should have been present at the meetings, noting the second was attended by Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore, who is leading more than a score of states in an assault on tobacco.
"Today's ruling was honestly the only legal conclusion that the judge could possibly have reached," Butler family attorney Langston told Reuters.

"The two allegations were that there was improper contact, which certainly wasn't supported. And secondly, that only one party had contact with the judge. Liggett, who is still a defendant, was present at every single moment of contact."

Tobacco attorneys say Liggett should not be considered a true defendant in the context of the meetings, because the company already had agreed to turn over internal documents and to cooperate with states suing other members of the industry.
The Butler case was scheduled to go to trial on August 18 in Landrum's court.

The two sides first would have to argue over whether or not to include the Liggett documents as trial evidence, however. The state Supreme Court has ordered a hearing on the question. Jones County court officials said no date has yet been set.
